Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Doctor
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event, Authority Presence: Police, Offender Cues: Seeing the offender
  Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement, Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed, Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power

Vignette:
Priya, a 51-year-old physician, often found her mind drifting back to that harrowing evening in the hospital’s dimly lit parking garage. She had been finishing up a late shift, the usual quiet of the building giving way to an unsettling stillness as she made her way to her car. The memory of the man who had suddenly emerged from the shadows, his scarred knuckles vivid as he grabbed her, was a constant torment. She could still recall the overpowering smell of stale cigarettes mixed with something metallic, like old blood, clinging to her nostrils even now. Afterwards, the arrival of the police, their uniforms stark against the flashing blue lights, had felt like a further intrusion, their questions blurring into an incomprehensible din. The entire experience had been so extreme, so out of sync with her ordered life, that she often felt the story was unreal, as if it had happened to someone else, not to a respected doctor like herself.

In the months that followed, Priya found herself trapped in a perpetual state of hypervigilance. The quiet hum of the hospital at night, once a familiar comfort, now made her feel that something dangerous was about to happen. Any unexpected or loud sound, whether a dropped tray in the cafeteria or a sudden burst of laughter from a colleague, would send a jolt of adrenaline through her, her body tensing as if bracing for impact. Even in the ordinary course of her work, when a new patient, a stranger, would approach her examination table, she would feel an intense surge of threat, her gaze darting, her breath catching. The sight of specific body parts, particularly men’s hands or forearms, could instantly transport her back to the assault, the terror of that moment returning with full force.

Her beliefs about how the world worked, about safety and predictability, had been completely shattered. Priya, who had always placed immense faith in human decency, had lost her faith in people, in life itself. She had come to believe that if she allowed herself to truly think about the event, to fully confront the horror, she would simply not be able to handle it. This conviction fueled a desperate need to avoid her thoughts. To cope, she discovered the fleeting escape of gambling. The thrill of the spin, the brief surge of excitement, served as a powerful distraction, a temporary reprieve from the relentless terror and intrusive memories. She would spend hours online or at the local casino, chasing that momentary oblivion.

At work, Priya started wearing increasingly concealing clothing – long-sleeved scrubs and high-collared undershirts – even in the warmth of the clinic, a subconscious attempt to avoid being noticed, to become invisible. She meticulously avoided any place or person that might remind her of the man who had harmed her, often taking circuitous routes to and from the hospital, declining social invitations that might put her in unfamiliar settings. These avoidance strategies, while offering fleeting relief, slowly began to erode her life. The gambling, initially a distraction, had started to strain her finances and created a growing distance in her marriage; her husband, bewildered by her withdrawal and secrecy, felt increasingly shut out. Her colleagues noticed her diminished engagement, her once-sharp focus often broken by her internal battles. The constant state of threat monitoring was utterly exhausting. Priya finally sought help not because she felt hopeful, but because the unbearable weight of her hidden life, the unyielding terror, and the accumulating consequences of her desperate coping had become too much to bear. She simply wanted the relentless fear to stop.
